title: Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff
summary: The container starts, exits, and Kubernetes keeps restarting it with growing delay.

steps.title: Confirm it is actually looping
steps.look: RESTARTS climbing over successive checks. A high but static count is an old incident, not a live one.

signals.means: This is a Job or a one-shot container that finished. restartPolicy is wrong, not the app.

steps.title: Read the previous container's logs
steps.look: The FIRST fatal line, not the last. Startup errors scroll off the top and the tail is usually just the shutdown noise.

signals.means: It died waiting on a dependency that was not reachable.
Required configuration was absent at startup.
The process cannot read a path or bind a port as its runAsUser.

steps.title: Read the termination state
steps.look: exitCode and reason. This is the single most decisive field in the whole runbook.

signals.means: The kernel killed it for memory. No amount of restarting will fix this.
The entrypoint was found but is not executable. Check the file mode in the image.
The entrypoint was not found at all. Wrong path, or missing shell in a distroless base.
The application chose to exit. The reason is in the logs, not here.

steps.title: Check whether a probe is doing the killing
steps.look: Events for 'Liveness probe failed'. If present, the app may be healthy but slow to start, and the probe is executing it.

signals.means: The liveness probe is killing a container that may only need more startup time.

causes.cause: A required env var, Secret key or ConfigMap key is absent, so the process exits during startup.
causes.fix: Fix the owning Deployment/Secret/ConfigMap in source control and reconcile. Do not patch the live Pod.

causes.cause: The container's memory limit is below its real working set.
causes.fix: Raise limits.memory in the owning Deployment, or fix the leak. Restarting will reproduce it every time.

causes.cause: A database, cache or upstream service was not reachable at startup.
causes.fix: Confirm the dependency's Service has endpoints, then decide whether the app should retry instead of exiting.

causes.cause: initialDelaySeconds is shorter than the app's real startup time, so liveness kills it mid-boot.
causes.fix: Move the slow-start allowance to a startupProbe rather than inflating the liveness delay.

causes.cause: Exit 127. The command in the image manifest does not exist at that path.
causes.fix: Check the Dockerfile ENTRYPOINT/CMD against the built image. A distroless base has no /bin/sh.

causes.cause: Exit 126. The file exists but lacks the execute bit, or its interpreter line is wrong.
causes.fix: Add chmod +x in the Dockerfile, or fix the shebang. Rebuild the image.

causes.cause: runAsUser cannot read a mounted path or bind a privileged port.
causes.fix: Correct fsGroup on the volume, or move the app to a port above 1024.

causes.cause: A one-shot workload is running under restartPolicy Always.
causes.fix: Run it as a Job with restartPolicy OnFailure or Never.

verify: RESTARTS holds steady across at least three checks spanning the app's normal startup window.
The container reports Ready, and readiness has not flapped in recent events.
The original failing request or job path completes successfully.
escalate: Image tag and digest, plus resources and probe definitions

title: Pod stays Pending and is never scheduled
summary: The Pod object exists but no node has accepted it.

steps.title: Read the scheduler's own reason
steps.look: The scheduler states exactly why each node was rejected, in the form '0/N nodes are available: ...'. Read that string before anything else.

signals.means: No node has enough free allocatable resource for the requests.
The nodeSelector or affinity rule matches no node's labels.
Every candidate node carries a taint this Pod does not tolerate.
This is a storage problem wearing a scheduling costume.

signals.match: (?i)node\(s\) didn't find available persistent volumes|volume node affinity conflict
signals.means: The PV is pinned to a zone the scheduler cannot place the Pod in.

steps.title: Compare the request against real allocatable capacity
steps.look: Requests, not usage. A node at 12% CPU usage can still be 100% requested and therefore unschedulable.

steps.title: Read what this Pod is actually asking for
steps.look: Compare these three against the previous step. The mismatch is usually obvious once both are on screen.

causes.cause: The sum of requests exceeds allocatable on every node.
causes.fix: Lower the request to the workload's real profile, or add capacity. Raising the limit does not help; the scheduler reads requests.

causes.cause: nodeSelector or nodeAffinity references labels no node carries, often after a node pool was replaced.
causes.fix: Correct the selector, or label the intended nodes. Check for typos in the label key first.

causes.cause: Nodes are tainted (NoSchedule) and the Pod has no matching toleration.
causes.fix: Add the toleration if the Pod belongs on those nodes, otherwise target a different pool.

causes.cause: A referenced PVC has not bound, so the Pod cannot be placed.
causes.fix: Follow the PVC Pending runbook. Nothing about the Pod spec will fix this.

causes.cause: An existing PV lives in one zone and the Pod cannot be scheduled there.
causes.fix: Use a topology-aware StorageClass with volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer.

verify: The Pod reports a nodeName and moves past Pending.
No new FailedScheduling events appear for this Pod.
The change was made in the owning manifest, not by editing the live Pod.
escalate: Allocated resources block from describe nodes
The Pod's requests, nodeSelector and tolerations

title: Service exists but returns connection refused
summary: DNS resolves the Service, but nothing answers. Usually the Service has no endpoints.

steps.title: Check whether the Service has any endpoints at all
steps.look: ENDPOINTS column. If it is empty or <none>, the Service is pointing at nothing and the problem is the selector or pod readiness, not the network.

signals.means: No pods are backing this Service.

steps.title: Compare the Service selector against real pod labels
steps.cmd: kubectl get svc {service} -n {namespace} -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}{"\n"}' && kubectl get pods -n {namespace} --show-labels
steps.look: An exact match on every key. One extra or renamed label is enough to produce an empty Service, and this is the most common cause by a wide margin.

signals.means: Compare character by character. 'app' and 'app.kubernetes.io/name' are different keys.

steps.title: Check whether the backing pods are Ready
steps.look: A pod that is Running but 0/1 Ready is excluded from endpoints. Readiness, not liveness, controls Service membership.

signals.means: The pod is up but failing readiness, so it is deliberately kept out of the Service.

steps.title: Confirm the target port matches the container port
steps.look: targetPort must match the container's real listening port, or a named port the container declares. port is what clients dial; targetPort is where it lands.

causes.cause: The Service selector does not match the pod labels.
causes.fix: Align them in the manifests. Changing the Deployment's pod labels forces a rollout, so prefer correcting the Service.

causes.cause: Pods are running but failing their readiness probe, so kube-proxy excludes them.
causes.fix: Fix the readiness endpoint or its threshold. The Service will populate on its own once pods report Ready.

causes.cause: targetPort points at a port nothing is listening on.
causes.fix: Set targetPort to the container's real port, or use a named port so the two cannot drift.

verify: EndpointSlice lists the expected pod IPs.
A request from inside the cluster to the Service name succeeds.
The count of endpoints matches the number of Ready replicas.

title: ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull
summary: The kubelet cannot fetch the image. The event message says which of four reasons.

steps.title: Read the pull failure message
steps.look: The Failed event's message. It names the exact reason, and each reason has a different owner.

signals.means: The tag does not exist in the registry.
The node has no valid credentials for this registry.
TLS trust failure between the node and the registry.
The node could not reach the registry at all.

steps.title: Check the image reference on the pod
steps.look: Typos in the registry host or tag are the single most common cause. Read it character by character.

steps.title: Check whether a pull secret is attached
steps.look: Empty output on a private registry means the pod has no credentials. The secret must live in the same namespace as the pod.

causes.cause: The tag does not exist in the repository.
causes.fix: Fix the tag in the manifest. Prefer pinning by digest for anything production.

causes.cause: No imagePullSecret, or it exists in a different namespace.
causes.fix: Create the secret in this namespace and reference it on the pod or its ServiceAccount.

causes.cause: The node does not trust the registry's certificate.
causes.fix: Install the CA on the nodes. Do not mark the registry insecure.

causes.cause: The node has no network path to the registry.
causes.fix: Check egress rules, the NAT gateway and any proxy configuration on the nodes.

verify: The pod moves past ImagePullBackOff and the container starts.
No new Failed pull events appear.
escalate: Whether an imagePullSecret is attached and in which namespace

title: Container was OOMKilled
summary: The kernel killed the container for exceeding its memory limit. Restarting reproduces it.

steps.title: Confirm it was memory and not an external kill
steps.look: OOMKilled specifically. Exit 137 alone only means SIGKILL, which something else could have sent.

signals.means: The kernel's OOM killer took it. This is a limit problem, not a crash.

steps.title: Read the configured limit
steps.look: Compare limits.memory against what the process actually needs. If requests and limits differ widely, scheduling and eviction behave in ways you may not expect.

steps.title: Look at actual usage while it runs
steps.look: Usage climbing steadily towards the limit points at a leak. Usage spiking at a particular operation points at a batch size or a large request.

steps.title: Check whether the whole node is under pressure
steps.cmd: kubectl describe node $(kubectl get pod {pod} -n {namespace} -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}') | grep -A5 Conditions
steps.look: MemoryPressure true means the node is squeezed and eviction is in play, which is a different problem from a single container's limit.

causes.cause: The limit is below the real working set.
causes.fix: Raise limits.memory in the owning Deployment. Measure first with kubectl top rather than guessing.

causes.cause: Memory grows without bound until the limit is reached.
causes.fix: Raising the limit only delays it. Profile the application; the limit is doing its job.

causes.cause: A JVM or Node process sized its heap against the node rather than the cgroup.
causes.fix: Set an explicit max heap, or use a runtime version that is container-aware.

causes.cause: The node is out of memory and evicting pods.
causes.fix: Check requests across the node. Under-requesting causes overcommit and cascading evictions.

verify: RESTARTS holds steady through a full workload cycle.
kubectl top shows headroom between usage and the limit.
escalate: kubectl top output over a few minutes

title: Deployment rollout never finishes
summary: kubectl rollout status hangs. New pods are not becoming ready, or the old ones will not go.

steps.title: Read the rollout condition
steps.look: The Progressing condition's reason. ProgressDeadlineExceeded means it gave up; that reason names the layer at fault.

signals.means: The new ReplicaSet never became available in time.
Still in progress. Give it the deadline before treating it as stuck.

steps.title: Find what the new pods are doing
steps.look: The newest pods. Pending means scheduling, CrashLoop means the app, 0/1 Running means readiness.

signals.means: Scheduling, not deployment. Follow the Pending runbook.
The new image does not start. Follow the CrashLoop runbook.
The container runs but fails readiness.

steps.title: Check whether a disruption budget is blocking removal
steps.look: ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS at zero means old pods cannot be evicted, so the rollout cannot proceed.

steps.title: Check the surge and unavailable settings
steps.look: maxSurge 0 with maxUnavailable 0 is a deadlock: nothing new can start and nothing old can stop.

causes.cause: The new image fails to start.
causes.fix: Roll back, then fix the image. kubectl rollout undo restores the previous ReplicaSet.

causes.cause: New pods run but never pass readiness.
causes.fix: Check the probe path, port and initial delay against the new image's real startup.

causes.cause: New pods cannot be placed.
causes.fix: Follow the Pending runbook. Often the surge replica has nowhere to go.

causes.cause: A PodDisruptionBudget forbids removing the old pods.
causes.fix: Relax minAvailable, or scale up so the budget can be satisfied during the roll.

causes.cause: maxSurge and maxUnavailable are both zero.
causes.fix: Set at least one of them above zero.

verify: kubectl rollout status returns successfully.
All replicas are on the new ReplicaSet and Ready.

title: Node is NotReady
summary: The node stopped reporting healthy. Pods on it will be evicted after the toleration window.

steps.title: Read the node's conditions
steps.look: Which condition is false or unknown. Ready Unknown means the kubelet stopped reporting entirely, which is very different from a pressure condition.

signals.means: The kubelet stopped posting status. The node may be gone or partitioned.
The node is out of disk.
The node is out of memory.
Process ID exhaustion, usually a fork loop.
The CNI has not configured the node's network.

steps.title: Check how long it has been unhealthy
steps.look: The age against the last transition. Pods are evicted after the not-ready toleration, five minutes by default.

steps.title: See what is still on it
steps.look: Anything not yet evicted. Stateful workloads here need attention before the node is replaced.

steps.title: Cordon it so nothing new lands
steps.look: The node shows SchedulingDisabled. Do this before investigating so the problem does not spread.
steps.note: Marks the node unschedulable. Running pods are not touched, but nothing new will be placed. Reverse with kubectl uncordon.

causes.cause: The kubelet is not posting status.
causes.fix: Check the host: is it up, is the kubelet service running, can it reach the API server.

causes.cause: The node's disk is full, often image or log growth.
causes.fix: Clear space, then set image garbage collection and log rotation so it does not recur.

causes.cause: The node is out of memory.
causes.fix: Look for pods without limits. Overcommit on requests is the usual root cause.

causes.cause: Process ID exhaustion.
causes.fix: Find the fork loop. Set a pid limit on the offending workload.

causes.cause: The CNI plugin has not initialised on the node.
causes.fix: Check the CNI DaemonSet's pod on that node.

verify: The node reports Ready.
Workloads have rescheduled and are serving.
The condition that flipped has a remediation, not just a restart.
escalate: Whether the host is reachable outside Kubernetes
Pods still bound to the node

title: PersistentVolumeClaim stays Pending
summary: The claim never binds, so every pod using it stays Pending too.

steps.title: Read the binding events
steps.look: The provisioner's own message. WaitForFirstConsumer is not an error at all; it is the expected state until a pod is scheduled.

signals.means: Normal. The volume binds when a pod that uses it gets scheduled.
The named StorageClass does not exist in this cluster.
Static provisioning with no matching PV.
The provisioner tried and the backend refused.

steps.title: Check the requested class and access mode
steps.look: ReadWriteMany is unsupported by most block storage drivers and is a common silent mismatch.

steps.title: List the classes that actually exist
steps.look: Whether the requested name exists, and which class is marked default. An empty storageClassName uses the default; a missing default leaves the claim Pending forever.

causes.cause: The class uses WaitForFirstConsumer.
causes.fix: Nothing is wrong. Schedule a pod that mounts it and it will bind.

causes.cause: The named class does not exist.
causes.fix: Correct the name, or install the class. Cluster migrations often leave stale names in manifests.

causes.cause: Static provisioning with no PV matching size, class and access mode.
causes.fix: Create a matching PV, or move to dynamic provisioning.

causes.cause: The driver does not support the requested access mode.
causes.fix: Use ReadWriteOnce for block storage, or a filesystem driver for ReadWriteMany.

causes.cause: The storage backend rejected the request, often on quota.
causes.fix: Read the provisioner's message and check the cloud-side quota.

verify: The PVC reports Bound with a volume name.
The pod that needed it is scheduled and running.
escalate: Requested class, size and access mode

title: DNS resolution fails inside pods
summary: Names do not resolve from within the cluster. Work out whether it is CoreDNS, the pod's resolver, or upstream.

steps.title: Test resolution of a cluster name from the pod
steps.look: An IP means cluster DNS works and the problem is narrower than you thought. Nothing means the resolver path is broken.

signals.means: Cluster DNS works. Test an external name next.
Cluster DNS is not answering for this pod.

steps.title: Check that CoreDNS is running
steps.cmd: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o wide
steps.look: All replicas Ready. CrashLooping CoreDNS is usually a bad Corefile edit or a resolver loop.

signals.means: CoreDNS itself is failing. Check its logs for a loop plugin detection.
CoreDNS is not ready, so nothing in the cluster resolves.

steps.title: Read the pod's resolver configuration
steps.look: The nameserver should be the cluster DNS Service IP. A node-level resolver here means dnsPolicy is wrong for a cluster workload.

signals.means: Normal, but it means short names try several search domains first, which looks like slow DNS under load.
The pod is using a node or public resolver, not cluster DNS.

steps.title: Test an external name
steps.look: Cluster names working but external failing points at CoreDNS's upstream forwarder or egress, not at Kubernetes DNS itself.

causes.cause: CoreDNS is unhealthy.
causes.fix: Read its logs. A loop plugin error means the upstream resolver points back at CoreDNS.

causes.cause: The pod uses host DNS instead of cluster DNS.
causes.fix: Set dnsPolicy ClusterFirst. hostNetwork pods need ClusterFirstWithHostNet explicitly.

causes.cause: CoreDNS cannot reach its upstream resolver.
causes.fix: Check the forward directive in the Corefile and egress from the CoreDNS pods.

causes.cause: Short names expand through five search domains before the real lookup.
causes.fix: Use fully qualified names with a trailing dot for hot paths, or tune ndots per pod.

causes.cause: A NetworkPolicy blocks egress to port 53.
causes.fix: Allow UDP and TCP 53 to kube-system in the policy.

verify: Both cluster and external names resolve from inside the pod.
CoreDNS replicas are Ready with no restarts.
escalate: Which names fail: cluster, external, or both

title: Ingress returns 502, 503 or 404
summary: The ingress answers but the backend does not. Each status points at a different layer.

steps.title: Identify which status you get and from whom
steps.look: The Server header tells you whether the ingress controller answered or something upstream did. 404 usually means no rule matched; 503 usually means no healthy backend.

signals.means: The controller matched a rule but has no healthy endpoint behind it.
No ingress rule matched this host and path.
The controller reached a backend and got an invalid response.

steps.title: Check the ingress has an address and correct rules
steps.look: An empty ADDRESS means no controller has claimed it, usually a missing or wrong ingressClassName.

steps.title: Check the backend service has endpoints
steps.look: Empty endpoints produce 503 every time. This is the most common cause by a wide margin.

signals.means: No pods behind the service. Follow the no-endpoints runbook.

steps.title: Read the controller's own logs
steps.look: The controller logs the upstream it chose and why it failed. This is more precise than anything you can infer from the client side.

causes.cause: The backend service has no ready endpoints.
causes.fix: Fix pod readiness or the service selector. The ingress is working correctly by refusing to send traffic nowhere.

causes.cause: Host or path in the request does not match any rule.
causes.fix: Check pathType. Prefix and Exact behave differently, and this catches people out constantly.

causes.cause: No controller claimed the ingress.
causes.fix: Set ingressClassName to a class that exists in the cluster.

causes.cause: The backend returned something the controller could not use.
causes.fix: Check the app's own logs. Often TLS expected on a plain-HTTP backend port.

causes.cause: The ingress points at a service port that does not exist.
causes.fix: Match the port name or number to the service definition.

verify: The URL returns the expected status from the application.
The controller logs show the correct upstream being selected.
escalate: The exact status and response headers
Controller log lines for the request

title: Pods are being Evicted
summary: The kubelet is reclaiming resources on a node under pressure. The eviction message names which resource.
aliases: the node was low on resource

steps.title: List the evicted pods and read the reason
steps.look: The message names the resource that ran out. That single word decides everything that follows.

signals.means: The pod wrote too much to its writable layer or an emptyDir.
The node ran out of memory and reclaimed the largest offender over its request.
The node exhausted inodes, usually many small files.

steps.title: Find which node is under pressure
steps.look: Which nodes report DiskPressure or MemoryPressure. If it is one node, it is a host problem; if it is all of them, it is a capacity problem.

steps.title: Check whether the evicted workload declared requests
steps.cmd: kubectl get pod {pod} -n {namespace} -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].resources.requests}' 2>/dev/null || echo 'pod already removed'
steps.look: Pods without requests are evicted first. Declaring a request is what buys a workload protection.

causes.cause: The container wrote more to local disk than its ephemeral-storage allowance.
causes.fix: Set an ephemeral-storage request and limit, and move logs to stdout rather than files.

causes.cause: The node ran out of memory.
causes.fix: Set memory requests on the workloads sharing that node. Eviction targets pods exceeding their request first.

causes.cause: Inode exhaustion from many small files.
causes.fix: Find the directory generating them. Log rotation usually solves it.

causes.cause: Best-effort pods are evicted first.
causes.fix: Declare requests so the workload gets a guaranteed or burstable class.

verify: No new evictions during a normal workload window.
The node's pressure conditions are false.
The affected workloads declare requests.
escalate: Whether the workload declares requests and limits
